title: Al-Layl: the night
hook: by the night and the day, your strivings are different (Surah 92)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last line of Ad-Duha. Your line was speak of the gift. Did you tell anyone one good thing that was given to you? Day one hundred eighty-nine.

Picture two people on the same street at eleven at night. Same darkness, same streetlight, same hour. One is driving home from a double shift so her kids can eat. The other is out to do something he'll hope nobody finds out about. From a satellite, they look identical: two dots moving in the dark. The night covers them both. What's different is where each one is going, and why. The surah just before Ad-Duha in the Qur'an opens on exactly that picture. Night and day, male and female, and then a sentence that could be written about any street, any office, any family group chat. Today: Al-Layl, the night.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, THE SAME DARK STREET.` → `THE NIGHT COVERS THEM BOTH.` → `AL-LAYL, THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-two begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the night enshrouding. The night that covers, that wraps things so you can't see them. Then by the day when it shines, and by the One who created the male and the female. Three oaths, and all of them are pairs: dark and light, one and the other. Then the point the oaths were leading to. Verse four says, in plain terms, your striving is scattered, diverse, going in different directions. The Arabic word for striving is sa'y. It's effort with your feet in it, the sense of hurrying toward something. The same root names the walk pilgrims make between the hills of Safa and Marwa during Hajj, retracing Hajar's run for water. And the word describing the effort, shatta, means scattered, spread apart, as different from each other as night from day. So the surah says: you are all under the same sky, but your efforts are not the same. Some run toward what's good. Some run away from it. The night hides the difference for a while. It doesn't erase it. Notice what the surah does not do. It doesn't say everyone's effort is wasted, or that effort is bad. It says effort has a direction. The next verses, which we'll open tomorrow, describe the two directions. Today is only the question. It's the end of a week, too. We began it with At-Tin, made in the best form, then Ash-Sharh, the chest opened and hardship paired with ease, then Ad-Duha, the morning, the orphan and the gift told out loud. Now the night, and the question under all of them: where is the effort going?
screen: `THREE OATHS, ALL IN PAIRS.` · `SA'Y — STRIVING, EFFORT WITH FEET.` · `SHATTA — SCATTERED, NOT THE SAME.` · `EFFORT HAS A DIRECTION.` · then, large: `EFFORTS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and for two minutes, look back over yesterday as if from above, like that satellite. Where did your effort actually go? Not where you meant it to go. Where it went. The phone, the work, a person, a worry. Don't judge it. Just notice the direction, the way you'd notice which way a river runs. The bell holds the time.
Al-Layl. The night, the name of Surah ninety-two, which swears by the night and the day and says your efforts differ. Today's word.
Your line: efforts differ. Once today, when you're about to spend real effort on something, ask which way it's pointed. Then keep going, or turn. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Al-Layl is one of the short surahs many Muslims learn by heart and recite in the prayer; its opening oaths, by the night and the day, are often read as a reminder that every person's effort is heading somewhere.

match.prompt: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
pairs: the walk called sa'y in Hajj

myth: Surah 92 says all human effort is wasted
it says efforts differ: they go in different directions, not that they're pointless.
the opening oaths of Al-Layl come in pairs
night and day, male and female: opposites, before the line about differing efforts.
sa'y shares a root with the walk between Safa and Marwa
both carry the sense of hurrying, striving toward something.

fork.setup: Al-Layl swears by the night, the day, and the creation of male and female. what does it say next?
options: that night is better than day
that the world will end at night
fork.reveal: your striving is scattered, going in different directions. the oaths in pairs set up the point: same sky, different directions.

original.note: Arabic: the night, the name of Surah 92, which opens by swearing by the night as it covers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about nighttime.
what it means: by night and day, male and female: your efforts differ, going in different directions.

what a scholar hears: sa'yakum la-shatta. sa'y is the word for the pilgrims' walk between Safa and Marwa; shatta means dispersed, the plural of shatit. the oaths in pairs mirror the two paths the surah goes on to describe.

sources.ref: Qur'an 92:2–4 (the day, male and female, your effort is diverse)
Qur'an 2:158 (Safa and Marwa); Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 (Hajar's search for water)

notes: Please confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 92:1 ('By the night enshrouding').
92:4 paraphrased as 'your striving is scattered, diverse'; confirm.
Link between sa'y in 92:4 and the sa'i of Hajj is a root link only; the rite's name is usually spelled sa'i. Confirm wording. Bukhari 3364 for Hajar cited from memory.
shatta as plural of shatit: confirm.
